entry: Operation that combines two [[Function (mathematics)|functions]] to form a new function. The composition f∘g, written (f∘g)(x) = f(g(x)), applies g first and then f. It is a special case of the composition of relations and shares its properties, including associativity, so parentheses may be omitted in chains of functions. Composition is generally not commutative, since f∘g and g∘f usually differ. In a strict sense, g∘f is defined only when the codomain of f equals the domain of g. The composition of one-to-one functions is one-to-one, and of onto functions is onto, so the composition of two bijections is a bijection. For invertible functions, (f∘g)⁻¹ = g⁻¹∘f⁻¹. The [[Chain rule]] gives derivatives of composite differentiable functions.

Branch of [[Mathematical analysis|mathematical analysis]] studying vector spaces with limit-related structure, such as a norm or topology, and the linear functions defined on them. It grew from the study of function spaces and transformations such as the [[Fourier transform]], and proved especially useful for differential and integral equations. The word *functional*, for a function whose argument is a function, was first used in Hadamard's 1910 book on the [[Calculus of variations|calculus of variations]]. The basic objects are complete normed vector spaces, called Banach spaces. [[Hilbert space|Hilbert spaces]], whose norm arises from an inner product, can be completely classified. The field is central to the mathematical formulation of [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]], [[Partial differential equation|partial differential equations]] and machine learning.

[[Programming paradigm]] in which programs are constructed by applying and composing functions. Functions are first-class values: they can be bound to names, passed as arguments and returned from other functions. Programs are written as declarative expressions rather than sequences of statements that update the running state. Purely functional programming treats all functions as pure: a pure function always returns the same result for the same arguments and has no side effects. Its proponents argue that this yields fewer bugs and makes programs easier to test and verify. The paradigm evolved from [[Lambda calculus|lambda calculus]], and [[Lisp (programming language)|Lisp]], developed in the late 1950s, was the first high-level functional language. Many languages now support functional styles, including [[Python (programming language)|Python]] and [[JavaScript]]. Haskell, Erlang and F# are among the functional languages in use today.

Group of homotopy classes of loops in a [[Topological space]], based at a chosen point. It records information about the basic shape, or holes, of a space, and it is the first and simplest [[Homotopy]] group. Two loops are combined by concatenation, traveling along one and then the other. Because homotopy equivalent spaces have isomorphic fundamental groups, the group is a homotopy invariant. The fundamental group of a space X is written π₁(X). [[Henri Poincaré]] defined it in 1895 in his paper *Analysis situs*; the concept had emerged in the theory of [[Riemann surface|Riemann surfaces]] through the work of [[Bernhard Riemann]] and Felix Klein.

Interaction in nature that appears not to be reducible to more basic interactions. Four are known: gravity, [[Electromagnetism]], the weak interaction and the strong interaction. Gravity and electromagnetism produce long-range forces that can be seen directly in everyday life, while the strong and weak interactions act at subatomic scales and govern nuclear interactions inside atoms. Within the [[Standard Model]], the strong interaction is carried by the [[Gluon]], which binds [[Quark|quarks]] into [[Hadron|hadrons]] such as protons and neutrons, and the weak interaction is carried by W and Z bosons that mediate radioactive decay. Electromagnetism is carried by the [[Photon]], which underlies chemical bonding and electricity. Gravity is attributed to the curvature of spacetime in Einstein's general theory of relativity. Efforts to combine all four into a [[Theory of everything]] continue.

Theorem stating that every non-constant [[Polynomial]] with complex coefficients has at least one complex root. Equivalently, the [[Complex number|complex numbers]] form an algebraically closed [[Field (mathematics)|field]], and a polynomial of degree n has exactly n complex roots when counted with multiplicity. Despite its name, the theorem is not fundamental to modern algebra, and it cannot be proved by purely algebraic methods, because it requires the intermediate value theorem and the continuity of polynomial functions. It is also called d'Alembert's theorem. [[Carl Friedrich Gauss|Gauss]] published a largely geometric proof in 1799 that had a gap, and Argand, an amateur mathematician, published the first rigorous proof in 1806.

Theorem stating that every integer greater than 1 is either prime or a unique product of primes, up to the order of the factors. For example, 1200 = 2⁴·3·5² has exactly four 2s, one 3 and two 5s in every factorization. Factors must be [[Prime number|prime]]: 12 = 2·6 = 3·4 shows that factorizations into composite numbers need not be unique. The theorem is also called the unique factorization theorem, and it is one of the main reasons why 1 is not considered a prime number. Its existence part traces back to [[Euclid]]'s *Elements*, and [[Carl Friedrich Gauss|Gauss]] gave the first known proof of uniqueness in Article 16 of his *Disquisitiones Arithmeticae*. The theorem fails for algebraic integers, one reason the proof of [[Fermat's Last Theorem]] was so difficult.

Theorem linking differentiation and integration as inverse operations. The first part states that, for a [[Continuous function|continuous]] function f, an antiderivative of f can be obtained as the [[Integral|integral]] of f over an interval with a variable upper bound. The second part states that the integral of f over a fixed interval equals the change in any antiderivative between the ends of the interval, which avoids numerical integration when an antiderivative can be found. Historically, its importance lay in recognizing that calculating areas and calculating gradients are closely related. James Gregory published a rudimentary geometric form, Isaac Barrow proved a more general version, and [[Isaac Newton]] completed the surrounding theory. [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz|Gottfried Leibniz]] systematized the work and introduced the notation used today.

Unwavering attachment to a set of irreducible beliefs, usually in religion. The term describes a tendency in which scriptures, dogmas or ideologies are applied with a strict literal interpretation, with a strong distinction between ingroup and outgroup and a desire to return to a previous ideal. Scholars of religion regard it as a largely modern phenomenon that reacts against [[Modernism|modernism]], secularism and liberal tendencies; the label can be pejorative. In Christianity, supporters coined the term to describe five classic theological beliefs, in opposition to Modernist theology. [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] fundamentalists have targeted other religious and ethnic groups, as in [[Myanmar]] and [[Sri Lanka]], and examples occur in Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana traditions.

Ceremony connected with the final disposition of a corpse, such as [[Burial|burial]], entombment or [[Cremation|cremation]], with its attendant observances. Funerary customs, the beliefs and practices a culture uses to remember and respect the dead, vary between cultures and religious groups. The final disposition may destroy the body, as with cremation or sky burial, or preserve it, as with mummification. Common secular motives include mourning the deceased, celebrating their life and supporting the bereaved. Religious funerals may help the soul reach the [[Afterlife|afterlife]], [[Resurrection|resurrection]] or [[Reincarnation|reincarnation]]. A memorial service or celebration of life is held without the remains. Funeral rites date to at least 300,000 years ago, before modern *Homo sapiens*, and [[Neanderthal]] graves containing flower pollen have been found, though the evidence is not unequivocal.

[[Disease]] caused by fungi, also known as mycosis. Infections are traditionally divided into superficial, subcutaneous and systemic types, and the systemic ones, such as cryptococcosis and aspergillosis, are the most serious. Infection follows when [[Spore|spores]] are inhaled, touch the skin or enter through a cut, wound or injection. It is more likely in people with a weak [[Immune system|immune system]], such as those with [[HIV/AIDS]] or those taking steroids or cancer treatments. The [[Yeast|yeast]] *Candida albicans* can live in people without symptoms, but it can also cause severe systemic candidiasis. Diagnosis relies on signs, microscopy, culture and sometimes biopsy, and treatment usually uses antifungal creams or oral and injected medicines. Fungal infections affect more than one billion people every year, and an estimated 1.7 million deaths from fungal disease were reported in 2020.

Islamic kingdom in what is now [[Sudan]], northwestern Eritrea and western Ethiopia (1504–1821). It was founded by Sultan Amara Dunqas, a convert to Islam who built its capital, Sennar, on the [[Blue Nile]] and succeeded the medieval [[Nubia|Nubian]] kingdoms of Makuria and Alodia. The Funj people, an Arabized people of unclear ethnic origin, ruled a diverse population including Nubians, Beja, Bedouin and Hamaj. The sultanate reached its peak in the late 17th century, extending from the Third Cataract to the western fringes of the [[Ethiopian Highlands]] and east to the [[Red Sea]]. It encouraged Islam by inviting Sufi holy men. After the Hamaj seized power in a coup in 1762, the sultanate declined and broke up in civil wars. In 1821 the last sultan was forced to surrender to the Turco-Egyptian conquest.

Music genre that originated in African-American communities in the mid-1960s. It deemphasizes melody and chord progressions in favor of a strong rhythmic groove built on a bassline and a drum part, often at slower tempos than other popular music. Early funk, mainly through [[James Brown]], fused [[Jazz|jazz]] and [[Blues|blues]] and added a syncopated drum groove, emphasizing the first beat of each measure. In the late 1960s, Sly and the Family Stone and Parliament-Funkadelic broadened the genre, and groups such as Kool and the Gang and Earth, Wind & Fire developed it in the 1970s and 1980s. Funk derivatives include boogie, funk metal and G-funk, and Washington go-go is a funk subgenre. Funk samples and breakbeats have been used extensively in [[Hip-hop]] and [[Electronic dance music|electronic dance music]].

Soft, thick growth of hair covering the skin of almost all [[Mammal|mammals]]. It consists of oily guard hairs on top and a thick underfur beneath: the guard hairs keep moisture from the skin, and the underfur insulates. [[Thermoregulation]] is its primary purpose, but fur also gives protection, sensing, waterproofing and [[Camouflage|camouflage]]. Arctic mammals have dense fur; the dense underfur of the [[Muskox]] forms an airtight coat that allows survival at −40 °C (−40 °F). Desert camels use dense fur to keep solar heat off the skin, while aquatic mammals trap air in their fur to keep the skin dry. Seasonal color change in arctic animals such as the [[Arctic fox]] and [[Stoat]] is driven largely by camouflage. Mammals with reduced fur are called naked, as with the [[Naked mole-rat]].

Worldwide industry dealing in the acquisition and sale of animal [[Fur]]. Since a world fur market formed in the early modern period, the pelts of boreal, polar and cold temperate mammals have been most valued. The trade stimulated the exploration and colonization of [[Siberia]], northern North America, and the South Shetland and South Sandwich Islands. Russia was a major supplier of pelts to Western Europe before the colonization of the Americas, and from the 17th century until the late 19th century it was the world's largest supplier of fur. North America became a major supplier of beaver pelts for the [[Felt|felt]] hats of Europe in the 17th century. Today the trade is based on fur-farm pelts and regulated trapping, and it is controversial, with animal rights organizations opposing it.

Subculture defined by an interest in anthropomorphic animal characters. Members, called furries, often identify with personalized characters called fursonas and may wear fursuits at conventions. Socializing grew through the internet, including [[DeviantArt]]. The first furry conventions began in the 1970s, started by artists and fans at [[Science fiction|science fiction]] conventions. Stigma has led some members to hide their furry identity from family and coworkers.

Electrical safety device that provides overcurrent protection to a circuit. A fuse contains a metal wire or strip that melts when too much current flows through it, interrupting the current. It is a sacrificial device: once it has operated, it is an open circuit and must be replaced. A fuse can mitigate short circuits, overloads, mismatched loads and device failure, and wiring regulations usually set a maximum fuse rating for a circuit. The element is made of zinc, copper, silver, aluminum or alloys and may be surrounded by [[Sand|silica sand]] to quench the arc. Fuses were used from the early days of electrical engineering, and [[Thomas Edison|Edison]] patented one in 1890. [[Circuit breaker|Circuit breakers]] have replaced fuses in many contexts, but fuses remain where space, resiliency or cost matter.

Electricity generation from heat released by [[Nuclear fusion|nuclear fusion]] reactions. Research on fusion reactors began in the 1940s. As of 2025, only the National Ignition Facility in the United States has demonstrated a fusion energy gain factor above one. Experimental reactors burn [[Deuterium|deuterium]] and [[Tritium|tritium]], and tritium is scarce on Earth, decaying with a [[Half-life|half-life]] of about 12.3 years. Magnetic confinement uses [[Magnetic field|magnetic fields]] to hold [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]], while inertial confinement compresses fuel pellets with lasers. Fusion produces minimal high-level radioactive waste.

American animated science fiction [[Sitcom|sitcom]] created by [[Matt Groening]] for [[Fox Broadcasting Company|Fox]]. It follows Philip J. Fry, who is cryogenically preserved for 1,000 years and revived on December 31, 2999, and works at the Planet Express delivery company alongside Leela and the [[Robot|robot]] Bender. After Fox canceled the series, it was revived by Comedy Central and later by Hulu. It received critical acclaim, winning nine Annie Awards and six Emmy Awards.

[[Time]] after the past and the present. In special relativity, the future is the absolute future, or future light cone, and the flow of time depends on the observer's frame of reference. Presentism holds that only the present exists, so the future is unreal, while eternalism holds that past and future things exist eternally. Predeterminism holds that the past, present and future have already been decided. Religions consider the future in discussions of [[Karma]], life after death and eschatology. Future studies, or futurology, postulates possible futures, stressing plural futures rather than one monolithic future. [[Time dilation]] from special relativity would let fast-moving travelers advance into the future, and some physicists propose a [[Wormhole|wormhole]] as a time machine.

Projected long-term future of [[Earth]]. Plate tectonics is expected to form a [[Supercontinent]] in 250–350 million years. In about 600 million years, carbon dioxide levels will fall below those needed for trees' C3 photosynthesis. In about one billion years, the Sun's luminosity will be 10% higher, causing runaway evaporation of the oceans. The Sun is expected to become a [[Red giant]] in about 7.6 billion years, and Earth may be engulfed by it. Human technology, such as climate engineering, is an uncertain factor.

Artistic and social movement that originated in Italy in the early 20th century. It emphasized dynamism, [[Speed|speed]], [[Technology|technology]], youth and [[Violence|violence]], and objects such as the [[Car|car]], the airplane and the industrial city. Its key figures included Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, Umberto Boccioni, Carlo Carrà, Giacomo Balla and Luigi Russolo. Marinetti's Manifesto of Futurism, published in 1909, launched the movement, and Futurists worked in painting, sculpture, architecture, music, theater and cuisine. Futurism influenced [[Art Deco]], Constructivism, [[Surrealism]] and [[Dada]], and its artists rejected museums and the cult of the past. Parallel movements arose in the Russian Empire.

City (pop., 2020: 8,291,268), capital of [[Fujian]] province, China, lying between the Min River estuary and the city of Ningde. In 2020, 72.49% of inhabitants lived in urban areas. Fuzhou is a major center of scientific research and appears among the global top 50 cities tracked by the Nature Index. It is home to Fuzhou University and other public universities, including Fujian Normal University. The name derives from Mount Fu, a mountain said to lie northwest of the city, combined with the suffix -zhou, meaning settlement. In 1276 the city was renamed Fu'an Prefecture and designated the temporary imperial capital when the young Emperor Duanzong ascended the throne there.

Azerbaijani poet, regarded as one of the greatest poets of Turkic literature. Born Muhammad bin Suleyman, he took the pen name Fuzuli and wrote in Azerbaijani, Persian and Arabic. He composed poetry for patrons of the [[Aq Qoyunlu]] and [[Safavid dynasty|Safavid]] states as well as the Ottoman Empire, and wrote most of his poetry during Ottoman rule of Iraq. His best-known work is the lyric poem *Leylī va Macnūn*, an interpretation of a Middle Eastern tale of tragic love. His [[Ghazal|ghazals]] are known for their intense expression of feeling and their [[Mysticism|mystic]] metaphors. He played a role in elevating Azerbaijani poetry and language, and his work has been characterized as a reconciliation of Azerbaijani, Persian and Arabic literary practices and of Shia and Sunni beliefs. He died of the plague and was buried in Karbala.

Russian philosopher, novelist, short-story writer and journalist. His novels include *Crime and Punishment* (1866), *The Idiot* (1869), *Demons* (1872) and *The Brothers Karamazov* (1880). His *Notes from Underground* (1864) is considered one of the first works of [[Existentialism|existentialist]] literature. Arrested in 1849 for belonging to the Petrashevsky Circle, a group that discussed banned books critical of tsarist Russia, he was sentenced to death, but the sentence was commuted at the last moment. He then spent four years in a [[Siberia|Siberian]] labor camp, which inspired *The House of the Dead*. He later worked as a journalist and wrote *A Writer's Diary*. His books were translated into over 170 languages and influenced [[Anton Chekhov|Chekhov]], [[Albert Camus|Camus]] and [[Jean-Paul Sartre|Sartre]]. [[Friedrich Nietzsche|Nietzsche]] called him "the only psychologist from whom I had something to learn."
